items.followUp: Describe the role of photosystem I and photosystem II in the light reactions, and show the path of electrons.

rubric.why: Identifies light absorption at photosystem II and the splitting of water to replace its electrons.
rubric.description: PSII absorbs light; water is split, releasing oxygen, protons and electrons.
rubric.how: Award for linking PSII/light to water splitting or oxygen release.

rubric.why: Shows that electron transfer between the photosystems provides energy for ATP formation.
rubric.description: Electrons pass through an electron transport chain and energy is used to make ATP.
rubric.how: Award when electron transport and ATP formation are both stated.

rubric.why: Identifies PSI and the final reduction of NADP⁺.
rubric.description: Light excites PSI (P700); electrons ultimately reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
rubric.how: Award when PSI/light and NADPH production are connected.

rubric.why: The requested Z-scheme must show the electron path through both photosystems to NADPH.
rubric.description: Z-scheme shows electrons moving from water through PSII, the electron transport chain and PSI to NADP⁺; light raises electron energy at each photosystem.
rubric.how: Award for a labeled scheme or clearly ordered pathway containing both photosystems and the final NADPH step.

modelAnswer: Light is absorbed by photosystem II (P680), exciting electrons; photolysis of water replaces these electrons and releases oxygen and protons.
Electrons pass along an electron transport chain from PSII towards photosystem I; the released energy helps form ATP.
Light excites electrons in photosystem I (P700); they pass to ferredoxin and help reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
Z-scheme (energy rises upward): H₂O → PSII (P680) ↗ primary acceptor → electron transport chain (ATP formed) → PSI (P700) ↗ primary acceptor → ferredoxin → NADP⁺ reductase → NADPH.

items.followUp: Compare the structure and function of capillaries and veins.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the direction in which blood flows in arteries and veins.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood towards the heart.
rubric.how: Award when both directions are correctly compared.

rubric.why: Compares the wall structure of the two vessels.
rubric.description: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls; veins have thinner walls.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast in wall thickness or structure.

rubric.why: Compares the lumen sizes, an important structural difference.
rubric.description: Arteries have a narrower lumen; veins have a wider lumen.
rubric.how: Award for correctly comparing lumen size.

rubric.why: Recognises a functional or structural distinction related to blood pressure and flow.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood at higher pressure and generally lack valves; veins have valves to prevent backflow.
rubric.how: Award for either correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood towards the heart.
Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen; veins have thinner walls and a wider lumen.
Blood flows through arteries under high pressure; blood in veins is at lower pressure.
Veins have valves to prevent backflow; arteries generally do not have valves along their length.

items.followUp: Define ecosystem and name two components of an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Defines the biosphere as the region of Earth in which life occurs.
rubric.description: The biosphere is the zone or part of Earth where life exists.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the biosphere as Earth's life-supporting zone.

rubric.why: Shows the extent of the biosphere across Earth's environments.
rubric.description: It includes the parts of land, water and lower atmosphere inhabited by organisms.
rubric.how: Award for naming at least two of these environments or equivalent wording.

modelAnswer: The biosphere is the zone of life on Earth—the part of Earth where organisms live.
It includes life-supporting regions of land, water and the lower atmosphere.

items.followUp: What is an organ? Explain how cells are organised to form a tissue.

rubric.why: States what a cell is in relation to living organisms.
rubric.description: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of an organism.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the cell as the basic unit of life or structure.

rubric.why: Defines a tissue by its cells and their shared function.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.how: Award when both a group of cells and a shared function are conveyed.

modelAnswer: Cell level: a cell is the basic structural and functional unit of an organism.
Tissue level: a tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.

items.followUp: What are qualitative observations? Give one example.

rubric.why: Explains that quantitative observations use measurements or numerical data.
rubric.description: Quantitative observations are observations expressed in numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning numerical or measured data.

rubric.why: Provides a suitable numerical example of a measured observation.
rubric.description: Example: a person's temperature is 37°C, or a plant is 10 cm tall.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant example that includes a quantity or measurement.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are observations expressed as numbers or measurements.
Example: a plant is 10 cm tall.

items.followUp: What is a hypothesis? Briefly explain how it is tested.

rubric.why: Explains that a deduction is a logical conclusion or prediction made from a hypothesis.
rubric.description: A deduction is a logical conclusion or prediction drawn from a hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award for linking a logical conclusion, inference or prediction to a hypothesis.

rubric.why: Shows that deductions can be stated as testable consequences of a hypothesis.
rubric.description: A deduction states what should happen if the hypothesis is correct and can be tested.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning a testable consequence or an if–then prediction.

modelAnswer: A deduction is a logical conclusion or prediction drawn from a hypothesis.
It states what should happen if the hypothesis is correct and can be tested.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a threatened species and an extinct species?

rubric.why: Defines extinction as the complete disappearance of a species.
rubric.description: An extinct species has no living individuals remaining.
rubric.how: Award for stating that none of the species remain alive.

rubric.why: Distinguishes an endangered species as one that still exists but faces a high risk of extinction.
rubric.description: An endangered species still exists but is at risk of becoming extinct.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the species remains but is threatened with extinction.

modelAnswer: An extinct species has no living individuals remaining.
An endangered species still exists but has a very small or declining population and is at risk of extinction.

items.followUp: Differentiate between producers and consumers in an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Identifies flora as the plant life of a region.
rubric.description: Flora refers to the plants of a particular area or region.
rubric.how: Award for identifying flora with plant life.

rubric.why: Identifies fauna as the animal life of a region.
rubric.description: Fauna refers to the animals of a particular area or region.
rubric.how: Award for identifying fauna with animal life.

modelAnswer: Flora means the plants or plant life of a particular region.
Fauna means the animals or animal life of a particular region.
